sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam (AKA Glorious Leader) reports

We had the annual Farmers’ Dinner at The Knight’s Table, Stainforth on 17th October. What a great night! This is the event where we invite all the farmers each year to thank them for the use of their land, enabling us to indulge in our sport. Without them, our flying in the Dales would be very different - having club sites gives us easy access to known big sites for club coaching days - enabling us to fulfil our main aim of organising and promoting safe free flying in the Dales.  Long live the farmers! Although we invite all the farmers/landowners each year, there is usually a core group accept the invitation, and this year was no exception with 24 farmers/partners and 13 club members/guests in attendance. A cracking night. The noise in the room from the loud conversations from start to finish evidenced the convivial atmosphere, and the food as usual at club member Chris Maudsley’s establishment was fantastic. Well done all involved for hosting such a successful and important event for the club. I would encourage more members to consider attending when you see it advertised next year, definitely a worthwhile night.

So, November has arrived, the XCLeague is closed and with a deadline of 7th November to enter any recent flights, things are unlikely to change much in the league. Congratulations to our top guns Rich Meek (2nd), Jake Herbert (6th)  and Chris Fountain (9th) and Alex Colbeck (28th) in the national league. We can all bask in the reflected glory of leading the club standings for XC flying in the country. Give yourselves a pat on the back! Most of us of course can only dream of achieving flights such as the new Dales record 104km (312pts) set by Rich Meek and others in a 6hr+ flight from Cautley Spout on 10th May. Whilst we may rightly watch in awe at the achievements of flights such as this, the beauty of free flying is that you don’t have to set records to have the time of your life. A boat around at Cautley, with the main Dales peaks in sight, and the Howgills underneath you cannot fail to elate you, once you’ve got over the walk up of course! Cruising up and down the ridge from Windbank with the glory of Littondale stretched out before you and Wharfedale and beyond in sight? Yes please. The view down Dentdale as you fly at Brant Side? Our sites give us access to the most amazing experiences. Be thankful for your life choices that brought you this way, and give yourself another pat on the back! It doesn’t get much better.

The advent of November means that the AGM is looming. Clive’s notice in October Skywords, and on the forum (https://www.dhpc.org.uk/forum/viewtopic.php?t=3833) lay out what to expect in the coming month, and the agenda for the meeting itself is in this issue. Of most note is that after about 20 years of trying to reduce our working capital towards a minimum level, mainly by having no subs increase in that time, we are now at the target level. A small rise in subs is proposed. Thankfully, subs didn’t track inflation for the last 20 years, or they would now be around £48 a year!

See you at the AGM, if not on a hill before.

Fly safe everyone.

Tam

.

sections.title: Lessons from a Reserve Ride
sections.content:
In early to mid-September, I had a reserve ride while competing in the British and Irish Sports Class competition. I wanted to reflect on the experience, not just in terms of the usual advice to throw your washing early, but also on the things that helped me deal with the situation and the lessons I’ve taken away from it.

One thing I’m relieved about is that I wasn’t so task-focused that I failed to throw my reserve. I think attending the Cumbria Zip Line day, where you practise deploying your reserve on a zip line, was helpful. We had three rides on the course, and I’d also deployed my reserve for real on a zip line many years ago. Although I was unlucky that this happened to me, I recognise that my own lack of training in pitch control may have contributed to the incident.

Once I’d thrown the reserve, things started to go reasonably well. I managed to untangle it from the main wing, and I’m glad to say that the landing was very light. I was able to retrieve my reserve undamaged and walk fairly easily down the ridge to the first aider and comp organiser who were waiting to pick me up halfway down the hill.

The experience reinforced something for me: advice about throwing your reserve is of limited use on its own. Having the actions in your muscle memory, understanding what to do with your wing afterwards, and knowing that you may still have some control over the situation are all extremely valuable. An SIV course can help develop that understanding. Some pilots may not need one to learn these lessons, but I certainly did. I also wish I’d spent more time working on pitch control with two-liners. One SIV course on a 2 liner, for me, is obviously not enough.

The other thing this incident forced me to confront was my history of flying incidents. I won’t go into the details, but there have been a few incidents that, if another pilot had described them to me as a coach, would have caused me concern. The majority happened overseas. They weren’t always in competition, although competition was often part of the circumstances.

I don’t think competition pressure itself is necessarily the problem, or that it simply causes me to make poor decisions. Rather, I recognise that I’m often flying in a very unfamiliar environment, in air that I may not have experienced for years. We can be somewhat spoiled by the relatively mild conditions we often enjoy in the UK, but we also have our own distinctive flying environment. Personally, I’m comfortable flying in wind strengths that would be quite concerning to many Alpine or Iberian pilots. The reverse can also be true: conditions that feel familiar to pilots abroad may be outside our comfort zone.

When you consider the number of hours UK pilots spend flying abroad, incidents overseas are over represented given the smaller number of hours compared to the UK. They add up to a significant number, and we’ve seen the consequences reflected in insurance pricing over the past ten years or so.

So, what would I advise? First, work on your pitch control. An SIV course is an excellent way to develop those skills, and I wish I’d had more time practising with two-liners. Don’t assume that attending one course means you’ve finished learning.

Second, take it easy when flying abroad. You’re in a different flying environment, and you may find yourself feeling nervous, becoming tense or struggling to work out how to respond as a situation develops. Recognising that possibility before you launch is a useful first step towards managing it.

I noticed something during the competition at Saint-André. A number of pilots were beginning to sit out the later tasks as the demands of flying were taking their toll. For some, this was relatively early in their flying careers. In my view, Saint-André is a particularly demanding place to fly, with aerology that puts you right at the sharp end of Alpine paragliding. Knowing when to call it a day is part of being a good pilot. I sat out the rest of the week with a damaged wing and took my mind off flying with walking, friends, climbing and motorbiking. All in all not a waste but some lessons learned.

As the saying goes, slowly, slowly, catchy monkey with your flying in demanding alpine conditions. Have fun over the winter, and do keep getting out there on those calm, dry days. And don’t forget that we have a set of pilot exams coming up for anyone interested in working towards their Pilot Rating.

sections.title: AGM Notice 2026
sections.content:
Clive Sury reports

All members of the Dales Hang Gliding and Paragliding Club are invited to the AGM. Voting on committee proposals will only be possible in person at the meeting.

No proposals were received from members in response to the AGM notice in the October edition of Skywords.

AGENDA

1. Notes of 2025 AGM.

2. Adoption of reports from committee members.

Reports from committee members will be published on the website by the end of November and in the December edition of Skywords.

Members will be able to raise any questions regarding these at the AGM.

3. Approval of financial statement.

The Treasurer’s report for 2025/6 will be published on the website by 19th November, including proposed expenditure for 2026/7. As per the club constitution accounts shall be opened for inspection by any member of the club at any reasonable time.

4. Subscriptions 2025/6.

Committee proposal:

i. Membership fees to increase by £5 (£30/£27.50 for prompt payment).

ii. Contributions to the Flying Fund to remain at 35% of subscription income.

5. Revision of Club Constitution/Rules.

None.

6. Election of Officers.

All committee posts are up for re-election. You are welcome to stand for any post. All you need is a little spare time and a willingness to put something back into the club. No current committee member is going to be insulted if you want to put your name forward.

7. AOB.

Not for voting on.

Clive Sury

Secretary

3rd November 2026

Please note:

Following the formal business of the AGM, the annual awards for 2026 will be made – the prized club trophies and XC mugs. Come along to receive recognition of your success and help celebrate other members' achievements!

sections.title: Safety
sections.content:
Rob Urselmann reports

I would like to refresh everybody’s memories on when reporting an incident is either a must or a good idea.

Whilst I think everybody understands the need for a report when there is a serious accident (see point 1 below), there is also a lot of learning value in sharing your less severe or even simply “unwanted event” with the wider community.  If your experience (and maybe an article here in SkyWords) triggers somebody else to improve their practises that might just avoid a future accident.

The OSHA definitions for incident and accident are specific:

Incident: an unplanned, unwanted event with undesirable consequences

Accident: an incident resulting in serious injury and/or damage

Serious: more than 48h in hospital, fractures (except for finger, nose, toe), haermorrhage, ligament rupture.

When to report:

1.      It is a legal requirement that any accident involving an aircraft ('boarded with the intention of flight') must be reported to the police and the Air Accident Investigation Branch (AAIB) of the Department of Transport by the quickest available means. The BHPA investigates hang- and paragliding accidents on behalf of the AAIB. BHPA technical staff must be informed immediately if the incident is fatal, potentially fatal, or serious. Serious incidents include unusual equipment failures as well as accidents resulting in serious injury

a.          It involves injury, whether to participants or others.
        b.         It involves damage to property, third party or not.
        c.          It involves non-standard equipment or techniques.
        d.         It involves failed or malfunctioned equipment.
        e.          The emergency services were involved in the incident.
        f.        It may give rise to an insurance or legal claim

 

2.      Because the wider community can learn something from your incident
        -          It highlights safety points or was unusual.
        -          It's something you feel the sport may learn from.

Report an incident at https://report.bhpa-incidents.org/
